questions.q: Find the IQ of a child whose mental age and chronological age are given. Use the method 'Intelligence Quotient (IQ)'. Work with: chronological_age = 500, mental_age = 25. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of iq.
questions.a: 5 per cent

questions.q: Compute the IQ when MA equals 9 and CA equals 12. Use the method 'Intelligence Quotient (IQ)'. Work with: chronological_age = 1000, mental_age = 10. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of iq.
questions.a: 1 per cent

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Intelligence Quotient (IQ)' refers to.
questions.a: A single numeric index of general mental ability that compares what a test-taker can do at present (mental age) with how long the person has actually lived (chronological age), scaled so that an age-typical performer lands at 100.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Intelligence Quotient (IQ)'.
questions.a: Divide mental age by real age and multiply by 100; a result of 100 means performance typical of that age.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Intelligence Quotient (IQ)', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: iq = mental_age / chronological_age * 100

concepts.title: IQ Classification Bands and Population Shares

questions.q: Calculate the expected number of intellectually disabled persons in a district of 50000 using the IQ distribution. Use the method 'IQ Classification Bands and Population Shares'. Work with: band_percent = 15, population = 1200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of band_count.
questions.a: 180 units

questions.q: How many people out of one lakh would be expected to score above IQ 130? Use the method 'IQ Classification Bands and Population Shares'. Work with: band_percent = 25, population = 48000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of band_count.
questions.a: 12000 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'IQ Classification Bands and Population Shares' refers to.
questions.a: Because IQ scores pile up in the middle of a bell-shaped normal curve, psychologists label bands - average around 90-109, superior 120-130, borderline 70-79 - and can attach an approximate share of people to every band.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'IQ Classification Bands and Population Shares'.
questions.a: Multiply the total population by a band's percentage share to estimate how many people fall in that IQ band.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'IQ Classification Bands and Population Shares', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: band_count = population * band_percent / 100

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Intellectual Giftedness and Intellectual Disability' refers to.
questions.a: The two tails of the IQ spread get special labels: beyond 130 sits giftedness, exceptional general ability shown across many areas, while below 70 the term intellectual disability applies only when sub-average functioning is joined by deficits in adaptive behaviour during the developmental years up to 18.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Intellectual Giftedness and Intellectual Disability'.
questions.a: A low score alone never settles disability - adaptive behaviour deficits before adulthood must accompany it; giftedness also differs from talent, which is narrow excellence in one field.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Intellectual Giftedness and Intellectual Disability', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: iq_above_130 -> giftedness ; iq_below_70 plus adaptive_deficits within age_0_to_18 -> intellectual_disability

concepts.title: Psychometric Theories and the Guilford Cell Count

questions.q: How many cells does the structure-of-intellect model contain when its three dimensions are multiplied? Use the method 'Psychometric Theories and the Guilford Cell Count'. Work with: contents_count = 18, operations_count = 10, products_count = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of guilford_cells.
questions.a: 54000 units

questions.q: Calculate the total number of categories in Guilford's model from its operations, contents and products dimensions. Use the method 'Psychometric Theories and the Guilford Cell Count'. Work with: contents_count = 360, operations_count = 12, products_count = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of guilford_cells.
questions.a: 345600 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Psychometric Theories and the Guilford Cell Count' refers to.
questions.a: Structural theories treat intelligence as a set of measurable abilities: Spearman's general g-factor with specific s-factors derived through factor analysis, Thurstone's seven primary mental abilities, Jensen's Level I and Level II hierarchy, and Guilford's three-dimensional operations-contents-products model.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Psychometric Theories and the Guilford Cell Count'.
questions.a: Guilford crosses 6 operations with 5 contents and 6 products, so his structure-of-intellect model holds 180 ability cells.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Psychometric Theories and the Guilford Cell Count', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: guilford_cells = operations_count * contents_count * products_count

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligences' refers to.
questions.a: Gardner replaces one general ability with eight relatively independent kinds - linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic - so being strong in one tells you little about the rest.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligences'.
questions.a: Distinct intelligences work separately yet can cooperate on a real problem; each has a typical occupation profile.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligences', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: independent_intelligences = eight_types: linguistic, logical_mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily_kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic

questions.q: Using the method 'Sternberg's Triarchic Theory of Intelligence', work with: componential_analytical = 80, contextual_practical = 12, experiential_creative = 25. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of triarchic_intelligence.
questions.a: 117 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Sternberg's Triarchic Theory of Intelligence' and work with: componential_analytical = 60, contextual_practical = 300, experiential_creative = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of triarchic_intelligence.
questions.a: 560 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sternberg's Triarchic Theory of Intelligence' refers to.
questions.a: Sternberg reads intelligent behaviour as adapting to, shaping and selecting environments, and splits it into three strands: componential analysis that serves school success, creative use of experience on fresh problems, and practical coping with daily demands.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sternberg's Triarchic Theory of Intelligence'.
questions.a: Analytical intelligence predicts school grades, creative intelligence handles novel problems, and practical intelligence is street-smart dealing with the environment.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Sternberg's Triarchic Theory of Intelligence', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: triarchic_intelligence = componential_analytical + experiential_creative + contextual_practical

questions.q: Using the method 'PASS Model of Intelligence', work with: arousal_attention = 100, planning = 240, simultaneous_successive_processing = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of pass_units.
questions.a: 380 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'PASS Model of Intelligence' and work with: arousal_attention = 100, planning = 100, simultaneous_successive_processing = 24. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of pass_units.
questions.a: 224 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'PASS Model of Intelligence' refers to.
questions.a: Das, Naglieri and Kirby picture intellect as three brain-based functional units - arousal with attention, coding done either simultaneously or successively, and planning - all operating over a knowledge base; their Cognitive Assessment System tests these processes in ages 5 to 18.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'PASS Model of Intelligence'.
questions.a: Optimal arousal focuses attention, simultaneous processing integrates relations at once while successive processing stores information in sequence, and planning steers action to the goal.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'PASS Model of Intelligence', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: pass_units = arousal_attention + simultaneous_successive_processing + planning

concepts.title: Twin-Study Correlations: Nature and Nurture in Intelligence

questions.q: Using the method 'Twin-Study Correlations: Nature and Nurture in Intelligence', work with: corr_fraternal_together = 5, corr_identical_together = 500, corr_siblings_apart = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of correlation_gap.
questions.a: 300 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Twin-Study Correlations: Nature and Nurture in Intelligence' and work with: corr_fraternal_together = 10, corr_identical_together = 50, corr_siblings_apart = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of correlation_gap.
questions.a: 46 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Twin-Study Correlations: Nature and Nurture in Intelligence' refers to.
questions.a: Evidence on how intelligence develops comes from twin and adoption figures: the closer the genetic bond and the more similar the rearing setting, the higher the correlation between two people's intelligence scores, which supports a joint heredity-environment account.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Twin-Study Correlations: Nature and Nurture in Intelligence'.
questions.a: Identical twins reared together correlate near 0.90 while siblings reared apart correlate near 0.25, so genes set a range that environment fills in.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Twin-Study Correlations: Nature and Nurture in Intelligence', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: correlation_gap = corr_identical_together - corr_siblings_apart

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Aptitude: Nature and Measurement' refers to.
questions.a: Aptitude is a person's specific capacity to acquire a particular skill after training; it differs from intelligence (general mental ability) and from interest (mere preference), and it is measured with independent tests or multi-area batteries such as the DAT and GATB.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Aptitude: Nature and Measurement'.
questions.a: Aptitude predicts future performance; without both aptitude and interest in the same field, the outcome stays unsatisfactory.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Aptitude: Nature and Measurement', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: skill_outcome = aptitude_potential plus_training_environment

concepts.title: Creativity and Its Relation to Intelligence

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Creativity and Its Relation to Intelligence' refers to.
questions.a: Creativity is the power to bring forth something novel, appropriate and useful - a fresh solution, invention or composition; it rests on some minimum intellectual base, but past that base higher intelligence does not by itself ensure creative work.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Creativity and Its Relation to Intelligence'.
questions.a: Intelligence tests reward convergent thinking with one right answer, while open-ended creativity tests reward divergent thinking that runs in many directions.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Creativity and Its Relation to Intelligence', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: creative_output -> novelty plus usefulness ; requires minimum_intelligence, beyond_base no strict_correlation
